title: The notion of a viscosity solution
preview: Recently I have been interested in a paper by Dabon and Osher on their algorithms of computing solutions to the Hamilton-Jacobi equations. The solution to such an equation, given in the Hopf-Lax formula, is a viscosity solution.  The notion also appears to be interesting on its own. Here I only aimed to grasp the basic idea of viscosity solutions, and consequently the materials here are mostly motivational and elementary.

This note is based on the first part of Bressan's notes "Viscosity solutions and Hamilton-Jacobi equations and optimal control problems", which quite suits my aim. I also like very much the part on Laplace equation in Luis Silvestre's notes "viscosity solutions and elliptic equations" for motivational purpose.

Recently I have been interested in a paper by Dabon and Osher on their algorithms of computing solutions to the Hamilton-Jacobi equations. The solution to such an equation, given in the Hopf-Lax formula, is a viscosity solution. The notion also appears to be interesting on its own. Here I only aimed to grasp the basic idea of viscosity solutions, and consequently the materials here are mostly motivational and elementary.

This note is based on the first part of Bressan's notes "Viscosity solutions and Hamilton-Jacobi equations and optimal control problems", which quite suits my aim. I also like very much the part on Laplace equation in Luis Silvestre's notes "viscosity solutions and elliptic equations" for motivational purpose.

1.1. A motivating example

Consider the equation

∣∇u∣2−1=0\displaystyle |\nabla u|^{2}-1=0∣∇u∣2−1=0

with the boundary data

u=0x∈∂Ω\displaystyle u=0\quad x\in\partial\Omegau=0x∈∂Ω

A solution can be provided by the distance function

u(x)=dist(x,∂Ω)\displaystyle u(x)=\text{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)u(x)=dist(x,∂Ω)

which is general not differentiable at every point. For simplicity, let us assume we are in 1 {1}1-D, Ω=(−1,1) {\Omega=(-1,1)}Ω=(−1,1). The equation is simplified to

∣ux∣−1=0(1) \displaystyle |u_{x}|-1=0 (1)∣ux​∣−1=0(1)

with u(−1)=u(1)=0 {u(-1)=u(1)=0}u(−1)=u(1)=0. A solution is given by 1−∣x∣ {1-|x|}1−∣x∣, which is not differentiable at zero. At first, one can ask for a "weak'' solution, by relaxing u {u}u to be only Lipschitz continuous and that (1) holds almost everywhere. However, we then lose the uniqueness of the solution: there are infinitely many weak solutions to the Equation (1).
On the other hand, one can obtain a solution (also in the "weak'' sense) via the method of vanishing viscosity. The viscosity approximation to Equation (1)

∣uxϵ∣−1=ϵuxxϵ\displaystyle |u_{x}^{\epsilon}|-1=\epsilon u_{xx}^{\epsilon}∣uxϵ​∣−1=ϵuxxϵ​

which as a parabolic PDE has smooth solutions. The term ϵuxxϵ {\epsilon u_{xx}^{\epsilon}}ϵuxxϵ​ is considered as a regulizer of the equation. Assuming the family of solutions {uϵ}ϵ>0 {\{u^{\epsilon}\}_{\epsilon>0}}{uϵ}ϵ>0​ is bounded and equicontinuous on compact seubsets of Ω {\Omega}Ω, we can conclude via Arzela-Ascoli theorem that

uϵj→u\displaystyle u^{\epsilon_{j}}\rightarrow uuϵj​→u

locally uniformly in Ω {\Omega}Ω, for some subsequence ϵj→0+ {\epsilon_{j}\rightarrow0^{+}}ϵj​→0+ and limit function u∈C(Ω‾) {u\in\mathcal{C}(\overline{\Omega})}u∈C(Ω). One can find in this case u(x)=1−∣x∣ {u(x)=1-|x|}u(x)=1−∣x∣. The method of vanishing viscosity is sometimes sensible with intuition supplied from physics. However, as the technique is not always available, one search for some characterising properties of the solutions. We will make this idea more precise in what follows.

Proposition 1 (Characterisation of subharmonic functions) Let u∈C2(Ω) {u\in\mathcal{C}^{2}(\Omega)}u∈C2(Ω), x∈Ω {x\in\Omega}x∈Ω. Then Δu≥0 {\Delta u\geq0}Δu≥0 if and only if

Proof: If u∈C2(Ω) {u\in\mathcal{C}^{2}(\Omega)}u∈C2(Ω) with Δu≥0 {\Delta u\geq0}Δu≥0 in Ω {\Omega}Ω, and Br(x)⊂Ω {B_{r}(x)\subset\Omega}Br​(x)⊂Ω, then the Stoke's theorem implies that

∫Br(x)Δudx=∫Sr(x)∂u∂νdS=rn−1∫S1(0)∂u∂r(x+ry)dS(y)=rn−1∂∂r∫S1(0)u(x+ry)dS(y)≥0\displaystyle \begin{array}{rcl} \int_{B_{r}(x)}\Delta udx & = & \int_{S_{r}(x)}\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}dS\\ & = & r^{n-1}\int_{S_{1}(0)}\frac{\partial u}{\partial r}(x+ry)dS(y)\\ & = & r^{n-1}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\int_{S_{1}(0)}u(x+ry)dS(y)\geq0 \end{array}∫Br​(x)​Δudx​===​∫Sr​(x)​∂ν∂u​dSrn−1∫S1​(0)​∂r∂u​(x+ry)dS(y)rn−1∂r∂​∫S1​(0)​u(x+ry)dS(y)≥0​

Since u {u}u is differentiable, ∫Sr(x)u(x)→u(x) {\int_{S_{r}(x)}u(x)\rightarrow u(x)}∫Sr​(x)​u(x)→u(x) as r→0+ {r\rightarrow0^{+}}r→0+, hence we obtain

u(x)≤ - ⁣ ⁣∫Sr(x)u(y)dS(y).\displaystyle u(x)\leq\def\avint{\mathop{\,\rlap{-}\!\!\int}\nolimits} \avint_{S_{r}(x)}u(y)dS(y).u(x)≤-∫Sr​(x)​u(y)dS(y).

Conversely, if Δu(x0)≤0 {\Delta u(x_{0})\leq0}Δu(x0​)≤0 for some x0∈Ω {x_{0}\in\Omega}x0​∈Ω, then the above argument shows that in a small neighborhood of x0 {x_{0}}x0​ the average is decreasing. □ \Box□

In light of this characterisation, we may now define subharmonic functions, or in other words Δu≥0 {\Delta u\geq0}Δu≥0, in a weak sense, to be the functions u {u}u such that

u(x)≤ - ⁣ ⁣∫Sr(x)u(y)dS(y)\displaystyle u(x)\leq\def\avint{\mathop{\,\rlap{-}\!\!\int}\nolimits} \avint_{S_{r}(x)}u(y)dS(y)u(x)≤-∫Sr​(x)​u(y)dS(y)

is satisfied, for for all r {r}r such that Sr(x)⊂Ω {S_{r}(x)\subset\Omega}Sr​(x)⊂Ω. Equivalently we may replace Sr(x) {S_{r}(x)}Sr​(x) by Br(x) {B_{r}(x)}Br​(x). One can show that under this definition the subharmonic functions are in general only upper semi-continuous. We can also define superharmonic functions to be the functions u {u}u such that −u {-u}−u is subharmonic. It follows that they are lower semi-continuous. Thus we see that if a function u {u}u is both subharmonic and superharmonic in the weak sense, then u {u}u will satisfy the mean value property

u(x)= - ⁣ ⁣∫Sr(x)u(y)dS(y)\displaystyle u(x)=\def\avint{\mathop{\,\rlap{-}\!\!\int}\nolimits} \avint_{S_{r}(x)}u(y)dS(y)u(x)=-∫Sr​(x)​u(y)dS(y)

or in other words, Δu=0 {\Delta u=0}Δu=0 in a weak sense, and u {u}u will be continuous (so even weakly harmonic functions are smooth). We shall illustrate some usefulness of this formulation.

Hence the set {x∈Ω:u(x)=M} {\{x\in\Omega:u(x)=M\}}{x∈Ω:u(x)=M} is both open and relatively closed. It follows that u {u}u is constant in Ω {\Omega}Ω and hence in Ω‾ {\overline{\Omega}}Ω by continuity. □ \Box□

1.3. Scenario setup

Below the fold we will explore what notion of a solution that will enjoy properties such as Corollary 3 and 4. This will be in large parallel to the development above, although we will be more focusing on the comparison side, rather than the maximal principle. For historical reasons, such solutions are called viscosity solutions, originally appeared in the work of Evans, Crandall and Lions. Indeed, it would more appropriate to describe this kind of solutions to be e.g. comparison solutions or something else.

For most of the time, we will try to formulate the definition of the viscosity solutions to the first order PDE

F(x,u,∇u)=0(3) \displaystyle F(x,u,\nabla u)=0 (3)F(x,u,∇u)=0(3)

where F:Ω×R×Rn→R {F:\Omega\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}}F:Ω×R×Rn→R is continuous, and Ω⊂Rn {\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}}Ω⊂Rn ia open and bounded. Then for the comparison principle we will turn to a very special class, namely the Hamilton-Jacobi PDE

u+H(x,∇u)=0.\displaystyle u+H(x,\nabla u)=0.u+H(x,∇u)=0.

To motivate the notions, suppose u∈C1(Ω) {u\in\mathcal{C}^{1}(\Omega)}u∈C1(Ω) is a classical subsolution at x0∈Ω {x_{0}\in\Omega}x0​∈Ω, i.e.

F(x,u,∇u)≤0\displaystyle F(x,u,\nabla u)\leq0F(x,u,∇u)≤0

holds for all points in a neighborhood U {U}U of x0 {x_{0}}x0​. Let φ∈C1(Ω) {\varphi\in\mathcal{C}^{1}(\Omega)}φ∈C1(Ω) be such that u(x0)−φ(x0)=0 {u(x_{0})-\varphi(x_{0})=0}u(x0​)−φ(x0​)=0 and u−φ {u-\varphi}u−φ attains local maximum at x0 {x_{0}}x0​ in U {U}U. Then calculus implies that

∇u(x0)=∇φ(x0)\displaystyle \nabla u(x_{0})=\nabla\varphi(x_{0})∇u(x0​)=∇φ(x0​)

and hence

F(x0,u,∇u)=F(x0,φ,∇φ)≤0(4) \displaystyle F(x_{0},u,\nabla u)=F(x_{0},\varphi,\nabla\varphi)\leq0 (4)F(x0​,u,∇u)=F(x0​,φ,∇φ)≤0(4)

in U {U}U. Similarly, if u {u}u is a classical supersolution at x0 {x_{0}}x0​, and let ψ∈C1(Ω) {\psi\in\mathcal{C}^{1}(\Omega)}ψ∈C1(Ω) be such that u−ψ {u-\psi}u−ψ attains local minimum at x0 {x_{0}}x0​ in U {U}U, we have

∇u(x0)=∇ψ(x0)\displaystyle \nabla u(x_{0})=\nabla\psi(x_{0})∇u(x0​)=∇ψ(x0​)

and

0≤F(x,ψ,∇ψ)=F(x,u,∇u)(5) \displaystyle 0\leq F(x,\psi,\nabla\psi)=F(x,u,\nabla u) (5)0≤F(x,ψ,∇ψ)=F(x,u,∇u)(5)

Combining the two, we conclude that u {u}u is a classical solution locally at x0 {x_{0}}x0​. However, since a solution in the classical sense (namely, a differentiable one) to the Drichilet problem (3) does not exist in general, one seeks to formulate a "weak'' problem. In light of inequalities (4) and (5), we will try to formulate their equivalents in a non-differentiable setting.

1.4. One sided differentials

Definition 5 Let u:Ω→R {u:\Omega\rightarrow\mathbb{R}}u:Ω→R be a function. The set of super-differentials of u {u}u at x∈Ω {x\in\Omega}x∈Ω is defined as

D+u(x):={p∈Rn:lim sup⁡y→xu(y)−u(x)−⟨p,y−x⟩∣y−x∣≤0}\displaystyle D^{+}u(x):=\left\{ p\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:\limsup_{y\rightarrow x}\frac{u(y)-u(x)-\langle p,y-x\rangle}{|y-x|}\leq0\right\}D+u(x):={p∈Rn:y→xlimsup​∣y−x∣u(y)−u(x)−⟨p,y−x⟩​≤0}

and the set of sub-differentials of u {u}u at x∈Ω {x\in\Omega}x∈Ω is defined as

D−u(x):={p∈Rn:lim inf⁡y→xu(y)−u(x)−⟨p,y−x⟩∣y−x∣≥0}\displaystyle D^{-}u(x):=\left\{ p\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:\liminf_{y\rightarrow x}\frac{u(y)-u(x)-\langle p,y-x\rangle}{|y-x|}\geq0\right\}D−u(x):={p∈Rn:y→xliminf​∣y−x∣u(y)−u(x)−⟨p,y−x⟩​≥0}

Roughly speaking, locally the function sits below the plane situated at x {x}x defined by p∈D+u(x) {p\in D^{+}u(x)}p∈D+u(x), and sits above the plane defined by p∈D−u(x) {p\in D^{-}u(x)}p∈D−u(x), whenever the sets are nonempty. They are linear approximations to the behavior of the function at certain point, although they are not neccessarily unique unless the function is differentiable. But we are able to extract a lot of information, by comparing the function to the more regular ones, with the same linear behavior (in fact, we can even get quadratic information).

Lemma 6 Let u∈C(Ω) {u\in\mathcal{C}(\Omega)}u∈C(Ω). Then

*- p∈D+u(x) {p\in D^{+}u(x)}p∈D+u(x) if and only if there is a function φ∈C1(Ω) {\varphi\in\mathcal{C}^{1}(\Omega)}φ∈C1(Ω) such that ∇φ(x)=p {\nabla\varphi(x)=p}∇φ(x)=p and u−φ {u-\varphi}u−φ has a local maximum at x {x}x;

  • p∈D−u(x) {p\in D^{-}u(x)}p∈D−u(x) if and only if there is a function ψ∈C1(Ω) {\psi\in\mathcal{C}^{1}(\Omega)}ψ∈C1(Ω) such that ∇ψ(x)=p {\nabla\psi(x)=p}∇ψ(x)=p and u−ψ {u-\psi}u−ψ has a local minimum at x {x}x;*

since σ {\sigma}σ is increasing. Hence the function

φ(y)=u(x)+⟨p,y−x⟩+ρ(2∣x−y∣)\displaystyle \varphi(y)=u(x)+\langle p,y-x\rangle+\rho(2|x-y|)φ(y)=u(x)+⟨p,y−x⟩+ρ(2∣x−y∣)

is C1 {\mathcal{C}^{1}}C1 and

φ(x)=u(x)∇φ(x)=p.\displaystyle \varphi(x)=u(x)\quad\nabla\varphi(x)=p.φ(x)=u(x)∇φ(x)=p.

Moreover, for ∣y−x∣<δ {|y-x|<\delta}∣y−x∣<δ we have

u(y)−φ(x)≤σ(∣y−x∣)∣y−x∣−ρ(2∣x−y∣)≤0\displaystyle u(y)-\varphi(x)\leq\sigma(|y-x|)|y-x|-\rho(2|x-y|)\leq0u(y)−φ(x)≤σ(∣y−x∣)∣y−x∣−ρ(2∣x−y∣)≤0

Hence u−φ {u-\varphi}u−φ attains a local maximum at x {x}x. By posibly adding ∣x−y∣2 {|x-y|^{2}}∣x−y∣2 to φ(x) {\varphi(x)}φ(x), we get that u−φ {u-\varphi}u−φ attains a strict local maximum at x {x}x. □ \Box□

Remark 1 In the following we would be considering the simple scenario when a sequence of solutions um→u {u_{m}\rightarrow u}um​→u converging uniformly. We would prefer strict local extrema because they are more stable under small perturbations. Imagine in a long and flat valley where any point could be chosen as a local minimum. Then it is clear that by a small perturbation one could get a drastically different location for the new local minimum. But if x {x}x is a strict local maximum of u−φ {u-\varphi}u−φ, one can show that there is a sequence of points xm→x {x_{m}\rightarrow x}xm​→x such that um−φ {u_{m}-\varphi}um​−φ has a local maximum at xm {x_{m}}xm​ for all m {m}m large enough.

The formulation in Lemma 6 allows us to do some quick check about our intuitions.

Lemma 7 Let Let u∈C(Ω) {u\in\mathcal{C}(\Omega)}u∈C(Ω). Then

*- If u {u}u is differentiable at x {x}x, then

$ \\displaystyle D^{+}u(x)=D^{-}u(x)=\\{\\nabla u(x)\\} $
  • If the sets D+u(x) {D^{+}u(x)}D+u(x) and D−u(x) {D^{-}u(x)}D−u(x) are both nonempty, then u {u}u is differentiable at x {x}x;
  • The sets Ω+={x∈Ω:D+u(x)≠∅} {\Omega^{+}=\{x\in\Omega:D^{+}u(x)\neq\emptyset\}}Ω+={x∈Ω:D+u(x)=∅} and Ω−={x∈Ω:D−u(x)≠∅} {\Omega^{-}=\{x\in\Omega:D^{-}u(x)\neq\emptyset\}}Ω−={x∈Ω:D−u(x)=∅} are dense in Ω {\Omega}Ω.*
